body:
It is not uncommon in plugins to want to have an action that:
- Requires a user input before being performed.
- Needs to be dot-repeatable: ask once, `.` should repeat without re-asking.
- Should work with multicursor.

The general guide is to follow an operator route of "expression mapping that sets 'operatorfunc' and returns `'g@'`", but:
1. Return `'g@l'` to not ask for the textobject (if action is not an actual operator).
2. Cache user input to not re-ask when dot-repeating.

This currently poses a problem with multicursor (and `:h edit-repeat`) support due to a documented limitation:

```
- An 'operatorfunc' that caches its |getchar()| input instead of re-reading it
  misbehaves at the extra cursors: the unconsumed input runs as a normal-mode
  key.
```

---

To make things more grounded, here is a simplified demo:

```lua
local user_input
local rhs = function()
  -- Reset cached user input to trigger asking for it.
  -- The input is usually asked via `vim.fn.getcharstr` or `vim.fn.input()`,
  -- but there can be other custom synchronous user input method (like
  -- 'mini.input' or via https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/40275).
  user_input = nil

  vim.o.operatorfunc = function()
    -- Ensure cached user input is up to date
    user_input = user_input or vim.fn.input({ prompt = 'Input: ' })

    -- Simple text edit for demo purposes
    local pos = vim.api.nvim_win_get_cursor(0)
    local text = { user_input .. user_input }
    vim.api.nvim_buf_set_text(0, pos[1] - 1, pos[2], pos[1] - 1, pos[2], text)
  end

  return 'g@l'
end
vim.keymap.set('n', 'sd', rhs, { expr = true })

-- Add this to `init.lua` for an easier and more informative repro
vim.api.nvim_buf_set_lines(0, 0, -1, false, { 'aaa', 'bbb' })
_G.log = {}
vim.api.nvim_create_autocmd('CmdAtom', { callback = function(ev) table.insert(_G.log, ev.data) end })
```

This currently works as: type `sd` to initiate, type+confirm input (like `o<CR>`), it adds the doubled input at cursor. Pressing `.` adds the same doubled input at cursor *because it replays `g@l` portion*. While doing this with active multicursor or `:h edit-repeat` will *replay `g@lo\r`*. This mismatch is a problem.

One solution that (currently) works here is to resolve user input *during expression mapping evaluation* (i.e. before returning `g@l`). **However**, it hits `:h map-expression` limitations (textlock in current and other buffers, etc.). It currently seems to work fine for a pure `vim.fn.getcharstr`, but not for something more complicated: `vim.fn.input` with ui2 enabled (#41654) or custom implementations that edit text in other buffers to visualize input.

---

What can be done here? There are several approaches that I can think of (from most to least favorable in my opinion):

1. Prefer using unresolved `ev.data.lhs` when replaying in multicursor and `:h edit-repeat` instead of resolved `ev.data.keys`. In this example it will lead to replaying `sdo\r` which should work correctly (`sd` will reset `user_input` and ask+consume `o<CR>`).

2. Lift the `:h map-expression` limitatinons and make plugins resolve user input during expression mapping. This is (probably) what's required for #41654. Ideally also needs a test in `mcursor_spec.lua` that resolving user input in expression mapping will work with multicursor.

3. Make dot-repeat replay with the user input. This seems to be very breaking.

(@justinmk, I tried to make this as concise as I could)

comment_data.body: Would it make sense to have an `is_cascading()` function like `reg_executing()` and `reg_recording()`? This would generalize beyond the operator case as well.

> have an `is_cascading()` function

I was thinking of updating `nvim_get_mode()` to return a `casacding` field

Isn't checking for `#vim.api.nvim_buf_get_extmarks(0, mc, 0, -1, { limit = 1 }) > 0` enough?

But besides that, the ability to check whether the operator is performing with multicursor active is a bit orthogonal to the issue. The problem here is that there is no way to fully replicate the workflow *if* multicursor or `:h edit-repeat` is active. Resolving user input during expression mapping restrictions has issues. If there were none, I don't think checking for active multicursor is even needed.

> Isn't checking for `#vim.api.nvim_buf_get_extmarks(0, mc, 0, -1, { limit = 1 }) > 0` enough?

"cascading" is only true during replay. not merely if cursors exist.



> is a bit orthogonal to the issue.

yes, just replying to the comment here

Unfortunately, there is also a case of a true operator (action that asks for textobject) that can not benefit from resolving user input during expression mapping.

The operator that acts on textobject/motion and requires a user input usually asks for exactly that order of keys. The most prominent case here is "add surrounding" operator: `<surround-map>` + `<textobject>` + `<surround-id>`. Like `saiw)` in 'mini.surround' or `ysiw)` in `vim-surround`.

The necessity of this order means that user input for surrounding id *must* be done after resolving expression mapping (after resolving textobject, in fact).

Here is an example:

```lua
local user_input
local rhs = function()
  user_input = nil

  vim.o.operatorfunc = function()
    user_input = user_input or vim.fn.input({ prompt = 'Input: ' })

    -- Simple "add same surrounding"
    local right = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_mark(0, ']')
    vim.api.nvim_buf_set_text(0, right[1] - 1, right[2] + 1, right[1] - 1, right[2] + 1, { user_input })

    local left = vim.api.nvim_buf_get_mark(0, '[')
    vim.api.nvim_buf_set_text(0, left[1] - 1, left[2], left[1] - 1, left[2], { user_input })
  end

  return 'g@'
end
vim.keymap.set('n', 'sa', rhs, { expr = true })
```

Here typing `sa` - `iw` - `o<CR>` wraps inner word with letters `o`. This is dot-repeatable, but doesn't work in multicursor since `CmdAtom` has resolved `keys` as `"g@iwo\r"`.

Resolving user input would change the order to `sa` - `o<CR>` - `iw`. Which works, but doesn't fit the established convention.

---

As resolving the keys during expression mapping is not the full proof approach, this limits my current ideas only to preferring `CmdAtom.data.lhs` over `CmdAtom.data.keys`.

Adjusting the operator to conditionally cache user input (like during multicursor cascade, which indeed is a bit different from checking for present cursors when doing dot-repeat) would *probably* work for multicursor, but not *quite* for `:h edit-repeat`. The latter would require temporarily setting custom flag (like `_G.is_super_dot_repeat = true`) and making sure that operator respects it (which hard to do if operator is not owned by the user).

> As resolving the keys during expression mapping is not the full proof approach,

`lhs` is also not foolproof. if it were then there would be no debate. 

we need to try to see what the limits are for resolving a reliable "RHS". LHS is an option that's available (and easy to switch to) once we have exhausted the limits of RHS. and discovering those limits improves the system in general. there's no rush.

> One solution that (currently) works here is to resolve user input _during expression mapping evaluation_ (i.e. before returning `g@l`). **However**, it hits `:h map-expression` limitations (textlock in current and other buffers, etc.).

I think lifting these restrictions will be easy.

> > One solution that (currently) works here is to resolve user input _during expression mapping evaluation_ (i.e. before returning `g@l`). **However**, it hits `:h map-expression` limitations (textlock in current and other buffers, etc.).
> 
> I think lifting these restrictions will be easy.

[Unfortunately, there is also a case of a true operator (action that asks for textobject) that can not benefit from resolving user input during expression mapping](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/41657#issuecomment-5542956936).

> The general guide is to follow an operator route of "expression mapping that sets 'operatorfunc' and returns `'g@'`", but:
> 
> 1. Return `'g@l'` to not ask for the textobject (if action is not an actual operator).
> 2. Cache user input to not re-ask when dot-repeating.

Where does this guidance come from?

> 3\. Make dot-repeat replay with the user input. This seems to be very breaking.

This is what https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/42040 does.

> > The general guide is to follow an operator route of "expression mapping that sets 'operatorfunc' and returns `'g@'`", but:
> > 
> > 1. Return `'g@l'` to not ask for the textobject (if action is not an actual operator).
> > 2. Cache user input to not re-ask when dot-repeating.
> 
> Where does this guidance come from?

Something that has worked (wonderfully) for at least five years. Don't quite remember where I learnt that from.

> > 3. Make dot-repeat replay with the user input. This seems to be very breaking.
> 
> This is what [#42040](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/42040) does.

😢 🤦

Replying to https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/42040#issuecomment-5794708068 :

> There is no obviously stated counter-example (when using `lhs` makes it not work, but `keys` magically does).

As a general policy, RHS (resolved `keys`) "degrades gracefully" by doing _less_ (and a single `u` reverts it), whereas LHS worst-case is unbounded (fails by doing _too much_, with side-effects that `u` cannot revert).

Multicursor-cascade is meaningful only for edits and motions. LHS may resolve to arbitrary excmds/Lua that *do make sense* at the primary, but not at cascade. The "resolved" RHS lets replay partially apply (or skip) if the user action involves unreplayable subatoms, whereas replaying LHS would be very broken. Similar to how ins-completion does not show a menu at every cursor, but it does cascade.

Examples where RHS replay behaves better than LHS:

- Jumps / global ops (absolute, not cursor-relative):
  - `nnoremap X Gdd`: RHS replays only dd, per cursor.
  - `nnoremap <Down> ]C` in follow-mode [#41995](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/41995): LHS would make each cursor jump to its neighbor.
  - `nnoremap u u` [#42037](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/42037): LHS-replay would undo N times.
- Editor state outside of current buffer
  - `nnoremap ]x <Cmd>cnext<CR>x`: LHS-replay would be nonsense.
    - RHS replay: `:cnext` runs once at primary; only `x` cascades.
  - `nnoremap X <Cmd>set wrap!<CR>x`: LHS-replay toggles N times, the result depends on N.
    - RHS replay: the `<Cmd>` is not cascaded.
  - `nnoremap X <Cmd>write<CR>`, window commands (`<C-w>v`), plugin "bookkeeping" like `u<Cmd>lua …<CR>` mentioned in [#42037](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/42037).
    - LHS would replay the opaque `<Cmd>` per-cursor.
- LHS meaning changes at replay-time.
  - `@q` macro would re-read per-cursor registers.
- Viewport-relative commands. `zt`/`<C-d>`/H/L/… in mapping.
  - Per-cursor replay would be nonsense bc cursors may be offscreen.
- Performance:
  - LHS replays the entire callback per-cursor, which can be very slow if it involves treesitter queries, LSP requests, etc.
  - RHS replays only the resolved normal commands.

Examples where LHS replay behaves better (and RHS replay is wrong):

- Conditional mappings, e.g. `nnoremap X <Cmd>if getline('.') =~ 'foo' \| normal! dd \| endif<CR>`.
  - Unblocked by [`setrepeat()` API](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/issues/42069).

Thanks, this makes it at least somewhat clearer.

> Multicursor-cascade is meaningful only for edits and motions. LHS may resolve to arbitrary excmds/Lua that _do make sense_ at the primary, but not at cascade. The "resolved" RHS lets replay partially apply (or skip) if the user action involves unreplayable subatoms, whereas replaying LHS would be very broken. Similar to how ins-completion does not show a menu at every cursor, but it does cascade.
> 
> Examples where RHS replay behaves better than LHS:

To be perfectly honest, although this behavior might make some practical sense, my reaction about finding out this is that it is too "magical" (and in some cases straight up what I'd expect the opposite). There is no documentation about subtle distinctions of "some parts of mappings do not replay at all cursors, yet some others do". The only thing in `:h multicursor` about this area is `- Normal-mode commands, Mappings, and even Macros (|@|) replay at each cursor.`, which somewhat contradicts the info here. Maybe clarifying this part a bit more will be useful?

<details><summary>Some thoughts I had about multicursor in general</summary>

I have had several occasions of thinking how I'd implement a "multicursor plugin". The most robust and intuitive design for me would have been a toggle-abble two state operation: 1) place cursors without any replay; 2) replay every key at cursors (maybe in fixed order depending on how they were placed). Although this would have required an explicit toggle to do stuff like `u`, this design feels a bit more intuitive. The new built-in one is also okay, but indeed is a bit "magical" once you start thinking about which stuff needs to be cascading and which don't.

</details>

---

All the non-performance motivation for `RHS vs LHS` seems to come from "decide which parts of the RHS to replay". Would it maybe be possible to decide/fallback to replaying `LHS` during cascade *if* there was any form of user input as part of `RHS`? With the logic of "user needs to input something for this LHS, better replay the keys verbatim".

I have a doc update on the way, but it has been intentionally vague to avoid committing to something while we are still discovering things (not to mention, there are many things in Vim that simply are accidental; if I were starting from zero, I would have chosen stronger constraints from the beginning, but we have to work with Vim's historical choices).

> my reaction about finding out this is that it is too "magical" 

It certainly would feel less magical (less delightful) if they have the same brain-dead behavior as macros. Replaying LHS is basically that. But macros already exist, so...

> All the non-performance motivation for `RHS vs LHS` seems to come from "decide which parts of the RHS to replay". Would it maybe be possible to decide/fallback to replaying `LHS` during cascade _if_ there was any form of user input as part of `RHS`? With the logic of "user needs to input something for this LHS, better replay the keys verbatim".

Is that a relaxation of your objection to https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/42040 ? :)

> thinking how I'd implement a "multicursor plugin". The most robust and intuitive design for me would have been a toggle-abble two state operation: 1) place cursors without any replay; 2) replay every key at cursors (maybe in fixed order depending on how they were placed). Although this would have required an explicit toggle to do stuff like `u`, this design feels a bit more intuitive. 

If you are asking about a `'cascade'` option, the door is not closed (Nvim 0.14 maybe), and seems orthogonal to this issue. Meanwhile I think a `'follow'` option makes sense for Nvim 0.13.

> a bit "magical" once you start thinking about which stuff needs to be cascading and which don't.

It's imperfect but it is needed. Similar story for `'inccommand' + :normal` ... somehow or other, Nvim needs to reason about (classify) its commands. Not doing so is just a cop-out.

> > All the non-performance motivation for `RHS vs LHS` seems to come from "decide which parts of the RHS to replay". Would it maybe be possible to decide/fallback to replaying `LHS` during cascade _if_ there was any form of user input as part of `RHS`? With the logic of "user needs to input something for this LHS, better replay the keys verbatim".
> 
> Is that a relaxation of your objection to [#42040](https://github.com/neovim/neovim/pull/42040) ? :)

It was not intended as such. The idea is only about how multicursor cascades, not the present dot-repeat behavior.

Replaying LHS directly when there is a user input involved in its (and/or RHS) capture will behave as closely to as if the user manually typed those keys at each cursor. With the example from this issue, replaying will use `saiw)` (which will read the user input because plugin will think this is a result of user typing `sa`) instead of `g@iw)` (which will still be replayed for dot-repeat; without any breaking changes).
